subject: First stub of the autoplot package

messages.author: d31339b95f6e694c
messages.subject: First stub of the autoplot package
parts:
Hi everyone,

A while ago I asked about best practices for developing packages, with the aim of developing an autoplot package to extend ggplot2's functionality. I got plenty of good suggestions and a first stub of implementation is now there:
https://github.com/jiho/autoplot
it implements fortify and autoplot methods for Principal Component Analysis, for both stats::prcomp and FactoMineR::PCA.

You can try it with
library("devtools")
install_github("autoplot", "jiho")
library("autoplot")
example("autoplot.pca")
?autoplot.pca
?fortify.pca
What I particularly like with the whole autoplot approach is having most of the plot made for you but still being able to add new mappings on the output. Hopefully that will seduce people other than me ;)

It's my first package and I tried to be as clean as possible while setting up the development environment to use testthat, roxygen2 etc., so that took some time. I would appreciate if the knowledgeable people on this list could have a look at the code and point at my mistakes (in particular, I am very unfamiliar with the whole namespace thing). I added comments with TODOs so that you can see where I am going. Oh, and I am not a native english speaker so do not hesitate to suggest better wording for the documentation!

Thanks in advance to everyone!

PS: By the way, the variables plot in the example suggests that coord_fixed() does not give an exact 1:1 aspect ratio. The unit circle looks slightly stretched horizontally to me. Is that just me?

Jean-Olivier Irisson

I will be trying this in the morning. Thanks for your efforts. I have used ggplot to plot PCA data previously and it does make very nice plots. I've been using pcaMethods from bioconductor. Perhaps I can help make a fortify for that. One issue with PCA in R is a seeming lack of missing data handling and cross validation. That and the data you pass to the PCA computation cannot have non numerical columns. Which means you strip it of factors that you then have to cabins back in order to use colors, shapes, and sizes to differentiate groups of data to visualize associations. 

Also, I never could figure out how to get a biplot scaled correctly and compute the hotellings circle though....

messages.subject: Re: First stub of the autoplot package
parts:
Hi Brandon,

Thanks for the feedback.

On 2012-Jul-05, at 23:18 , Brandon Hurr wrote:
>
> I will be trying this in the morning. Thanks for your efforts. I have used ggplot to plot PCA data previously and it does make very nice plots. I've been using pcaMethods from bioconductor. Perhaps I can help make a fortify for that. One issue with PCA in R is a seeming lack of missing data handling and cross validation.

I've more experience with FactoMineR. It replaces missing data with the column's mean, which effectively makes it zero weight. Now if there are quite a few missing points, the people behind FactoMineR also coded the package missMDA which imputes the missing data through iterative PCA. I've tested this and got mixed results depending on the shape of the data of course. But if you have good explanatory power on the PCA + missing data that is well spread-out, it works quite well.

I'm not sure what you mean by cross-validation; split the dataset in bits, and repeat the PCA on various combinations of the bits, to check how robust the results are? I guess the boot package can probably help.

> That and the data you pass to the PCA computation cannot have non numerical columns. Which means you strip it of factors that you then have to cabins back in order to use colors, shapes, and sizes to differentiate groups of data to visualize associations.

Again, FactoMineR lets you use qualitative supplementary variables; those are not used to compute the projection but they can then be projected into the observations space. Essentially, it projects the barycenter of each level of the factor.

But even without this, with the current code in autoplot, if you provide the data together with the model, you can map aesthetics to columns of the original data which where not necessarily used in the PCA:

d <- data.frame(a=runif(10), b=runif(10), c=runif(10), foo=factor(round(runif(10,1, 3))))
pca <- prcomp(d[,-4], scale=T)
library("autoplot")
autoplot(pca, data=d)
autoplot(pca, data=d, mapping=aes(shape=foo))

library("FactoMineR")
pca <- PCA(d, quali.sup=4, graph=F)
autoplot(pca)
autoplot(pca, mapping=aes(shape=foo))
> Also, I never could figure out how to get a biplot scaled correctly and compute the hotellings circle though....

I'm French so I've been raised since childhood to hate biplots ;)
More seriously, I don't know why, there's a cultural bias against biplots here so I did not even try to produce one yet. I seem to recall that Hadley did not like them too. Overall, having two separate plots with two very different scales on the same graphic does not seem like a good idea indeed.

messages.subject: Re: First stub of the autoplot package
parts:
I've been making a score plot function for my own package, based on ggplot2, but it is so specific that I have yet to make it a standalone. I will have a look at your code when time permits...

The hottelling statistics can be computed as: (For a data frame with each PC in a column)

simconf <- function(X, alfa=0.95){

df1 <- ncol(X)

df2 <- nrow(X)

R <- as.data.frame(matrix(0, nrow=df1, ncol=4))

for (i in 1:df1){

m <- mean(X[,i])

int <- sqrt((df1*(df2-1))/(df2-df1)*qf(alfa,df1,df2-df1))*sd(X[,i])

R[i,] <- c(m, int, m-int, m+int)

}

names(R) <- c("Mean", "+/-", "Lower limit", "Upper limit")

row.names(R) <- paste("PC", as.character(1:df1), sep="")

R

}


Sorry for the badly named variables...

I ended up scaling the variables in the biplot based on the Hottelling stats, so that the highest loading was placed ~5 % longer away from the centre than the circle... I don't think there is any best approach...

I have also created some evaluation plots, such as leverage vs. distance to model, which I think are nice to have around

Thanks for the effort - I'm seduced : )

I asked a local statistician (I'm a biologist) and his answer was the following...

Measures of Distance to model vary in name, Umetrics call it DModX, others call it orthogonal distance (OD) and others Q statistsic

 

In “Multivariate Statistical Analysis in Chemometrics” by Kurt Varmusa he mentions a formula as follows:

OD = ||xi-P.t’||

Hubert et al 2005 take (median(OD^2/3)+MAD(OD2/3)*z0.975)^3/2 where z0.975 is the 97,5% quantile of the normal distribution as the critical OD


Happy to help add features to this PCA autoplot. I would like to try and make a fortify for pcaMethods PCA() and add some other plots like DModX (if we can get the calculations right). I would like to see an r^2 vs q^2 plot (crossvalidation, window-blinds or random). 

I don't know if fits into the autoplot package or something else entirely though...

Brandon

On 2012-Jul-05, at 23:18 , Brandon Hurr wrote:
>
> I will be trying this in the morning. Thanks for your efforts. I have used ggplot to plot PCA data previously and it does make very nice plots. I've been using pcaMethods from bioconductor. Perhaps I can help make a fortify for that. One issue with PCA in R is a seeming lack of missing data handling and cross validation.

I've more experience with FactoMineR. It replaces missing data with the column's mean, which effectively makes it zero weight. Now if there are quite a few missing points, the people behind FactoMineR also coded the package missMDA which imputes the missing data through iterative PCA. I've tested this and got mixed results depending on the shape of the data of course. But if you have good explanatory power on the PCA + missing data that is well spread-out, it works quite well.

I'm not sure what you mean by cross-validation; split the dataset in bits, and repeat the PCA on various combinations of the bits, to check how robust the results are? I guess the boot package can probably help.

> That and the data you pass to the PCA computation cannot have non numerical columns. Which means you strip it of factors that you then have to cabins back in order to use colors, shapes, and sizes to differentiate groups of data to visualize associations.

Again, FactoMineR lets you use qualitative supplementary variables; those are not used to compute the projection but they can then be projected into the observations space. Essentially, it projects the barycenter of each level of the factor.

But even without this, with the current code in autoplot, if you provide the data together with the model, you can map aesthetics to columns of the original data which where not necessarily used in the PCA:

d <- data.frame(a=runif(10), b=runif(10), c=runif(10), foo=factor(round(runif(10,1, 3))))
pca <- prcomp(d[,-4], scale=T)
library("autoplot")
autoplot(pca, data=d)
autoplot(pca, data=d, mapping=aes(shape=foo))

library("FactoMineR")
pca <- PCA(d, quali.sup=4, graph=F)
autoplot(pca)
autoplot(pca, mapping=aes(shape=foo))
